source_refs.note: Book p. 192-194: 10.6 Triple Angle Identities, statements (i)-(iii), proofs, Examples 11-13; stops before Exercise 10.3. Misprints: 'os 2a' and two tan 3a lines in the proofs, Example 12(ii) 'sin 2t'.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: So far you have formulas for \(\sin 2\alpha\), \(\cos 2\alpha\), \(\tan 2\alpha\) (10.4) and for half angles (10.5). Triple angle identities do the same job for \(3\alpha\): they write \(\sin 3\alpha\), \(\cos 3\alpha\) and \(\tan 3\alpha\) using only functions of \(\alpha\). The whole idea of every proof below is one line: \(3\alpha = 2\alpha + \alpha\). Then the sum formulas of 10.3 and the double angle formulas of 10.4 do the rest.

blocks.text_alt: sine of 3 alpha equals 3 sine alpha minus 4 sine cubed alpha, identity (i)
cosine of 3 alpha equals 4 cosine cubed alpha minus 3 cosine alpha, identity (ii)
tangent of 3 alpha equals 3 tangent alpha minus tangent cubed alpha, over 1 minus 3 tangent squared alpha, identity (iii)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Notice the pattern: \(\sin 3\alpha\) is written only in \(\sin\alpha\), \(\cos 3\alpha\) only in \(\cos\alpha\), and \(\tan 3\alpha\) only in \(\tan\alpha\). That is why each proof chooses a particular form of \(\cos 2\alpha\) and replaces \(\cos^{2}\alpha\) or \(\sin^{2}\alpha\) using \(\sin^{2}\alpha + \cos^{2}\alpha = 1\).
Quick check with \(\alpha = 30^{\circ}\): \(\sin 90^{\circ} = 3\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) - 4\left(\frac{1}{8}\right) = \frac{3}{2} - \frac{1}{2} = 1\). Correct.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why \(\cos 2\alpha = 1 - 2\sin^{2}\alpha\) here? We want the answer in \(\sin\alpha\) only, so we pick the form of \(\cos 2\alpha\) that contains only \(\sin\alpha\). For the same reason \(\cos^{2}\alpha\) is replaced by \(1 - \sin^{2}\alpha\). Finally the like terms are collected: \(2\sin\alpha + \sin\alpha = 3\sin\alpha\) and \(-2\sin^{3}\alpha - 2\sin^{3}\alpha = -4\sin^{3}\alpha\).

(ii) In the same way, using \(\cos(A + B)\):
\[\cos 3\alpha = \cos(2\alpha + \alpha)\]
\[= \text{os}\ 2\alpha\cos\alpha - \sin 2\alpha\sin\alpha\]
\[= (2\cos^{2}\alpha - 1)\cos\alpha\]
\[\quad - 2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha\sin\alpha\]
\[= 2\cos^{3}\alpha - \cos\alpha - 2\sin^{2}\alpha\cos\alpha\]
\[= 2\cos^{3}\alpha - \cos\alpha\]
\[\quad - 2(1 - \cos^{2}\alpha)\cos\alpha\]
\[= 2\cos^{3}\alpha - \cos\alpha - 2\cos\alpha + 2\cos^{3}\alpha\]
\[\cos 3\alpha = 4\cos^{3}\alpha - 3\cos\alpha\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the second line of proof (ii) the book prints "os 2α cos α" (the letter c is missing). It is \(\cos 2\alpha\cos\alpha - \sin 2\alpha\sin\alpha\), the expansion of \(\cos(2\alpha + \alpha)\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Here we want the answer in \(\cos\alpha\) only, so we use \(\cos 2\alpha = 2\cos^{2}\alpha - 1\) and replace \(\sin^{2}\alpha\) by \(1 - \cos^{2}\alpha\). Collecting: \(2\cos^{3}\alpha + 2\cos^{3}\alpha = 4\cos^{3}\alpha\) and \(-\cos\alpha - 2\cos\alpha = -3\cos\alpha\).

(iii) Using \(\tan(A + B) = \frac{\tan A + \tan B}{1 - \tan A\tan B}\) and \(\tan 2\alpha = \frac{2\tan\alpha}{1 - \tan^{2}\alpha}\):
\[\tan 3\alpha = \tan(2\alpha + \alpha)\]
\[= \dfrac{\tan^{2}\alpha + \tan\alpha}{1 - \tan^{2}\alpha\,\tan\alpha}\]
\[= \dfrac{\dfrac{2\tan\alpha}{1 - \tan^{2}\alpha} + \tan\alpha}{1 - \dfrac{2\tan\alpha}{1 - \tan^{2}\alpha}\cdot\tan\alpha}\]
\[= \dfrac{2\tan\alpha + \tan\alpha - \tan^{3}\alpha}{1 - \tan^{2}\alpha - 2\tan^{2}\alpha}\]
\[\tan^{3}\alpha = \dfrac{3\tan\alpha - \tan^{3}\alpha}{1 - 3\tan^{2}\alpha}\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Proof (iii) has two misprints. (1) The second line is printed with \(\tan^{2}\alpha\) where \(\tan 2\alpha\) is meant; it should read \(\tan 3\alpha = \dfrac{\tan 2\alpha + \tan\alpha}{1 - \tan 2\alpha\tan\alpha}\). (2) The last line is printed as \(\tan^{3}\alpha = \dots\); the left side must be \(\tan 3\alpha\) (tan of three alpha, not tan alpha cubed): \(\tan 3\alpha = \dfrac{3\tan\alpha - \tan^{3}\alpha}{1 - 3\tan^{2}\alpha}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The step the book does not show: after putting \(\tan 2\alpha = \frac{2\tan\alpha}{1 - \tan^{2}\alpha}\), we have fractions inside a fraction. Multiply the numerator and the denominator of the big fraction by \(1 - \tan^{2}\alpha\):
numerator: \(2\tan\alpha + \tan\alpha(1 - \tan^{2}\alpha) = 3\tan\alpha - \tan^{3}\alpha\)
denominator: \((1 - \tan^{2}\alpha) - 2\tan^{2}\alpha = 1 - 3\tan^{2}\alpha\).
The formula holds whenever \(\tan\alpha\) and \(\tan 3\alpha\) are defined (so \(1 - 3\tan^{2}\alpha \ne 0\), e.g. \(\alpha \ne 30^{\circ}\)).

The next three examples practise the double angle formulas of 10.4 together with these ideas: replacing \(\sin 2\theta\), \(\cos 2\theta\) by forms in \(\theta\), and using \(\cos^{2}\theta = \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}\).

blocks.title: Example 11
steps:
Given: the identity to prove.
To prove: \(\dfrac{\sin\theta + \sin 2\theta}{1 + \cos\theta + \cos 2\theta} = \tan\theta\).
Method: start from the L.H.S. (the more complicated side). Write \(\sin 2\theta\) and \(\cos 2\theta\) in terms of \(\theta\), then factorise numerator and denominator and cancel the common factor.

Step 1: Expand the double angles
\[\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\]
\[\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^{2}\theta - 1\]
Why: of the three forms of \(\cos 2\theta\) we choose \(2\cos^{2}\theta - 1\), because its \(-1\) cancels the \(+1\) in the denominator.

Step 2: Substitute in the L.H.S.
\[\text{L.H.S.} = \dfrac{\sin\theta + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{1 + \cos\theta + 2\cos^{2}\theta - 1}\]
\[= \dfrac{\sin\theta + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\cos\theta + 2\cos^{2}\theta}\]
Why: \(1 - 1 = 0\) in the denominator.

Step 3: Take common factors
\[= \dfrac{\sin\theta(1 + 2\cos\theta)}{\cos\theta(1 + 2\cos\theta)}\]
Why: \(\sin\theta\) is common above and \(\cos\theta\) is common below; the same bracket \((1 + 2\cos\theta)\) appears in both.

Step 4: Cancel and simplify
\[= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tan\theta = \text{R.H.S.}\]
Why: a common non-zero factor \((1 + 2\cos\theta)\) can be cancelled, and \(\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tan\theta\) by definition.

Check: take \(\theta = 45^{\circ}\).
\[\text{L.H.S.} = \dfrac{\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + 1}{1 + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + 0} = 1\]
and \(\tan 45^{\circ} = 1\). Both sides agree.

blocks.title: Example 12
steps:
Given: the two formulas to show.
To prove: (i) \(\sin 2\theta = \frac{2\tan\theta}{1 + \tan^{2}\theta}\), (ii) \(\cos 2\theta = \frac{1 - \tan^{2}\theta}{1 + \tan^{2}\theta}\).
Method: the right sides contain only \(\tan\theta\). So write the left side as a fraction over \(1 = \cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta\), then divide numerator and denominator by \(\cos^{2}\theta\) to turn every term into \(\tan\theta\).

(i) Step 1: Write \(\sin 2\theta\) as a fraction over 1
\[\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \dfrac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{1}\]
\[= \dfrac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta}\]
Why: \(\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta = 1\), so the value does not change, but now the denominator can be turned into \(1 + \tan^{2}\theta\).

(i) Step 2: Divide above and below by \(\cos^{2}\theta\)
\[= \dfrac{\frac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta}}{\frac{\cos^{2}\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta} + \frac{\sin^{2}\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta}}\]
\[= \dfrac{2\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}}{1 + \tan^{2}\theta}\]
\[\sin 2\theta = \dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1 + \tan^{2}\theta}\]
Why: dividing the numerator and the denominator by the same non-zero number keeps the fraction equal; \(\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tan\theta\) and \(\frac{\sin^{2}\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta} = \tan^{2}\theta\).

(ii) Step 1: Write \(\cos 2\theta\) as a fraction over 1
\[\cos 2\theta = \cos^{2}\theta - \sin^{2}\theta\]
\[= \dfrac{\cos^{2}\theta - \sin^{2}\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta}\]
Why: same idea as in (i); we use the form \(\cos^{2}\theta - \sin^{2}\theta\) because both terms become \(\tan\) terms after dividing by \(\cos^{2}\theta\). (In the next printed step the book writes the denominator as \(\cos^{2}\theta + \sin 2\theta\); it must be \(\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta\), see the Book correction.)

(ii) Step 2: Divide above and below by \(\cos^{2}\theta\)
\[= \dfrac{\frac{\cos^{2}\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta} - \frac{\sin^{2}\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta}}{\frac{\cos^{2}\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta} + \frac{\sin^{2}\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta}}\]
\[\cos 2\theta = \dfrac{1 - \tan^{2}\theta}{1 + \tan^{2}\theta}\]
Why: each term divided by \(\cos^{2}\theta\) gives \(1\) or \(\tan^{2}\theta\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Example 12(ii), in the step where numerator and denominator are divided by \(\cos^{2}\theta\), the book prints the denominator as \(\cos^{2}\theta + \sin 2\theta\). It must be \(\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta\) (which equals 1); the next printed step already uses \(\frac{\sin^{2}\theta}{\cos^{2}\theta}\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: The results of Example 12 are worth remembering: they express \(\sin 2\theta\) and \(\cos 2\theta\) through \(\tan\theta\) alone. Dividing them also gives \(\tan 2\theta = \frac{2\tan\theta}{1 - \tan^{2}\theta}\), the formula of 10.4. They hold whenever \(\cos\theta \ne 0\).

blocks.title: Example 13
blocks.problem: Reduce \(\cos^{4}\theta\) to an expression involving only function of multiples of \(\theta\), raised to the first power.
steps:
Given: \(\cos^{4}\theta\).
To find: an equal expression that contains only \(\cos\theta\), \(\cos 2\theta\), \(\cos 4\theta\), ... each to the power 1 (no squares, no fourth powers).
Method: use the power-reducing form of the double angle formula, \(\cos^{2}\theta = \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}\), twice: once for \(\theta\) and once for \(2\theta\).

Step 1: The power-reducing formula
\[2\cos^{2}\theta = 1 + \cos 2\theta\]
\[\Rightarrow \cos^{2}\theta = \dfrac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}\]
Why: this comes from \(\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^{2}\theta - 1\). It changes a square into a first power of a double angle, which is exactly what the question wants.

Step 2: Write \(\cos^{4}\theta\) as a square and substitute
\[\cos^{4}\theta = (\cos^{2}\theta)^{2} = \left[\dfrac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}\right]^{2}\]
\[= \dfrac{1 + 2\cos 2\theta + \cos^{2}2\theta}{4}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{4}\left[1 + 2\cos 2\theta + \cos^{2}2\theta\right]\]
Why: \((a + b)^{2} = a^{2} + 2ab + b^{2}\) with \(a = 1\), \(b = \cos 2\theta\), and \(2^{2} = 4\).

Step 3: Reduce \(\cos^{2}2\theta\) again
\[\cos^{2}2\theta = \dfrac{1 + \cos 4\theta}{2}\]
\[\cos^{4}\theta = \dfrac{1}{4}\left[1 + 2\cos 2\theta + \dfrac{1 + \cos 4\theta}{2}\right]\]
Why: \(\cos^{2}2\theta\) is still a square. The same formula with \(2\theta\) in place of \(\theta\) gives \(\cos 4\theta\) (double of \(2\theta\)).

Step 4: Simplify
\[= \dfrac{1}{4\times 2}\left[2 + 4\cos 2\theta + 1 + \cos 4\theta\right]\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{8}\left[3 + 4\cos 2\theta + \cos 4\theta\right]\]
Why: take \(\frac{1}{2}\) out of the bracket by multiplying every term inside by 2; then \(2 + 1 = 3\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why would anyone want this? Powers like \(\cos^{4}\theta\) are hard to work with, while \(\cos 2\theta\) and \(\cos 4\theta\) to the first power are easy (later, in calculus, they are easy to integrate). The same method works for \(\sin^{4}\theta\) using \(\sin^{2}\theta = \frac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{2}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Every triple angle proof starts with \(3\alpha = 2\alpha + \alpha\).
2. \(\sin 3\alpha = 3\sin\alpha - 4\sin^{3}\alpha\) (only sines).
3. \(\cos 3\alpha = 4\cos^{3}\alpha - 3\cos\alpha\) (only cosines; the signs are the other way round).
4. \(\tan 3\alpha = \frac{3\tan\alpha - \tan^{3}\alpha}{1 - 3\tan^{2}\alpha}\).
5. Choose the form of \(\cos 2\alpha\) that fits the target: \(1 - 2\sin^{2}\alpha\) for sines, \(2\cos^{2}\alpha - 1\) for cosines.
6. \(\sin 2\theta = \frac{2\tan\theta}{1 + \tan^{2}\theta}\), \(\cos 2\theta = \frac{1 - \tan^{2}\theta}{1 + \tan^{2}\theta}\).
7. To remove powers use \(\cos^{2}\theta = \frac{1 + \cos 2\theta}{2}\) (and \(\sin^{2}\theta = \frac{1 - \cos 2\theta}{2}\)).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Mixing up the signs: \(\sin 3\alpha = 3\sin\alpha - 4\sin^{3}\alpha\) but \(\cos 3\alpha = 4\cos^{3}\alpha - 3\cos\alpha\). Check with \(\alpha = 0^{\circ}\): \(\cos 0^{\circ} = 1 = 4 - 3\).
2. Writing \(\sin 3\alpha = 3\sin\alpha\): the angle cannot be taken out of the sine.
3. Confusing \(\tan 3\alpha\) (tan of three alpha) with \(\tan^{3}\alpha\) (tan alpha cubed).
4. In Example 13, forgetting to reduce \(\cos^{2}2\theta\): the answer must have no squares.
